author: @AnkithaKaryam
text: Small Correction: Primitive arrays in Java store actual values contiguously in memory. For example, int[] arr = {10,20,30} is conceptually stored like |10|20|30|, which allows fast O(1) index access. Object arrays, however, store contiguous references, not the actual objects themselves. For example, String[] arr = {"A","B","C"} stores references together, while the actual "A", "B", and "C" objects may exist at different heap locations. So, primitive arrays have contiguous values, whereas object arrays have contiguous references.

text:
My learnings:

1. Why do we need Arrays?
Ans. Having a separate variable for each of 1000 elements will be tiring,
so we have Array in Java which allows us to store similar data type elements into a single reference variable
2. What is an array? What is array Index?
Ans. Array in Java allows us to store similar data type elements into a single reference variable
Each element can be accessed using an index which is 0-based
3. How do we declare arrays?
Ans. int[] days = new int[7];
4. How do we initialize arrays?
Ans. days = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7};
5. Can we modify an array element once it is assigned a value? If yes, how?
Ans. Yes, days[2] = 33;
6. How do you print size/length of an array?
Ans. using days.length property
7. How do we print a single array element and also an entire array? Explain with loop, toString()
Ans. We can iterate through each element of an array using for loop/forEach loop and also we can print using Arrays.toString(days);
8. How arrays works internally? Explain memory management?
Ans. the reference variable is stored in stack memory and it points to the first memory location of array elements in heap memory created at runtime.
Memory elements are contiguos
9. What is ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException? How can we overcome it?
Ans. If we try to access index of the array which does not exists we get this exception.
To overcome this we can use Arraylist which can dynamically vary its length based on requirement.

Misc questions:
1) If you pass an array to a method in Java, is it passed by value or passed by reference? What happens if the method modifies the array elements?
Ans. It is pass by reference so if we try to modify any element in other method that change will be reflected in original array also
2) Can we assign one array to another array directly in Java? If yes, what happens internally?
Ans. Yes, we can assign, but the new reference type will point to old object only
3) Can an array be final in Java? If yes, can we still modify its elements?
Ans. Yes Arrays can be final in java and we can modify its elements but we cannot point it to another object
4) What’s the difference between Arrays.equals(arr1, arr2) and arr1 == arr2?
Ans. equals() method will compare the actual elements of array one by one, but == will only compare memory location of the array object
5) Can you have a 0-length array in Java?
Ans. Yes

text:
03:35 📌 Arrays in Java are stored in the heap memory, and heap objects are not guaranteed to be continuous.

FOR THE ABOVE POINT

In Java, all objects (including arrays) are stored on the heap, but the heap itself does not guarantee that different objects will be laid out in a continuous block of memory. Here’s the key distinction:
1. Each Individual Array Is Contiguous Internally
• When you create an array (e.g., int[] arr = new int[5];), the elements of that specific array are stored in a contiguous block within the heap.
• This means, for arr[0] through arr[4], the memory cells for these five integers are next to each other.
2. Different Heap Objects Are Not Necessarily Adjacent
• The heap is managed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) and its Garbage Collector.
• As you allocate and free objects, the JVM finds free memory wherever available in the heap.
• Therefore, two different arrays (or any other objects) can be located at completely separate regions of the heap, not necessarily side by side.

🎯 Key Takeaways for quick navigation:

Arrays in Java are collections of data types, including primitives or objects, organized within square brackets [ ].
Syntax for array declaration involves specifying the data type followed by square brackets and the variable name.
The "new" keyword is used to dynamically allocate memory for arrays at runtime.
Arrays in Java have zero-based indexing, meaning the first element is accessed at index 0.
In Java, objects and non-primitive data types are stored in the heap memory, while primitives are stored in the stack memory.
Unlike in some other languages like C++, where array memory allocation is continuous, in Java, heap memory objects, including arrays, may not be contiguous.
The default value for uninitialized elements in an array of objects is "null," indicating no reference to an object.
Primitives in Java include int, char, boolean, float, etc., while non-primitives encompass complex data types like arrays and custom objects.
Objects in Java are stored in heap memory, while reference variables point to them from the stack memory.
Arrays in Java are collections of reference variables, and each element of the array points to an object in memory.
Arrays can be initialized and accessed using indexes, with the last index being size minus one.
For loops are commonly used to iterate over array elements for initialization or printing.
The enhanced for loop (for-each loop) simplifies array iteration by directly accessing elements.
The `length` variable of an array provides its size, facilitating dynamic array handling.
The `Arrays.toString()` method efficiently converts arrays to strings for printing.
Strings are immutable in Java, while arrays are mutable, allowing modification of array elements.
When passing arrays to functions in Java, a copy of the reference variable is made, allowing changes to the original array.
Multi-dimensional arrays in Java, like 2D arrays, are stored as arrays of arrays, with varying sizes for each dimension.
The length of an array in Java refers to the number of rows in a 2D array.
Each row of a 2D array can have a different number of columns, making column size specification optional.
Nested for loops are commonly used for inputting values into multi-dimensional arrays, with the outer loop iterating over rows and the inner loop over columns.

author: @sereneSoundtracks825
text:
Reference variables are present in the stack memory and the actual object that the reference variable points to is stored in the heap memory.

author: @anuragC819
text:
If anyone is wondering why it is O(1) in insertion, the logic (as best as I can understand), is this -
Basically every time you double it, the capacity increases to twice, so you need not double it for quite some time.
Suppose your original ArrayList had cap:10
And you have to fill 1000 values
After 5 values, new_cap = 20
After 10 values, new_cap = 40
After 20 values, new_cap = 80
After 40 values, new_cap = 160
After 80 values, new_cap = 320
After 160 values, new_cap = 640
After 320 values, new_cap = 1280

As this increases, you realize that to reach that half capacity when you need to double the size, that value also increases. To increase capacity to 2560, you need to add 320 more values. To increase capacity further to 5120, you need to add 640 more values

So for larger values, this basically becomes O(1) wherein it is assumed that the ArrayList size is already so big, you're just appending values
